value.overview: The Wattled Jacana (Jacana jacana) is a long-toed wetland bird of tropical South America. It uses its exceptionally long toes and claws to walk across floating leaves and other aquatic vegetation. Adults have a dark head and neck, chestnut-brown upperparts, yellow wing areas, and a brightly colored bill, facial shield, and wattle. Females are larger than males, and the species has unusual sex roles: females defend territories while males incubate eggs and care for chicks.
value.classification: The Wattled Jacana belongs to the family Jacanidae, the jacanas, within the shorebird order Charadriiformes. It is one of two regularly recognized Jacana species in the Americas, the other being the Northern Jacana (Jacana spinosa).
value.identification: This medium-sized jacana has a blackish head, neck, and breast, rich chestnut upperparts, and conspicuous yellow on the wings. The bill is yellow with a reddish facial shield and fleshy red wattle at its base. Long blue-gray legs and extremely elongated toes allow it to move over floating plants. It is similar to the Northern Jacana, but the two species differ in detailed head, wing, and body-color patterns. Juveniles are browner and less boldly marked.
value.rangeHabitat: The Wattled Jacana occurs widely in tropical South America east of the Andes, with a smaller range extending into western Panama and occasionally Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a very rare or accidental visitor rather than a regular resident; documented records include the southern Pacific lowlands near the Panamanian border. It favors shallow freshwater marshes, flooded fields, lagoons, ponds, slow-moving waters, and wetlands with abundant floating vegetation, generally in warm lowland areas.
value.migrationStatus: Mostly resident across its main South American range, although local movements may follow changing water levels. In Costa Rica it is not known as a regular seasonal migrant; occurrences are rare, irregular, and probably linked to dispersal from western Panama or nearby South American populations.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in shallow wetlands containing floating vegetation. The species has a reversed mating system: females are larger, defend territories, and may mate with several males, while males usually build or maintain floating nests, incubate the eggs, and care for the young. Nests are made from aquatic plants and may rest directly on floating leaves or among emergent vegetation. Chicks are precocial and can leave the nest soon after hatching, but remain under male protection.
value.dietFeeding: The Wattled Jacana feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates found on floating plants or at the water surface. Its diet can also include small mollusks, crustaceans, fish, seeds, roots, and other plant material. It walks slowly across aquatic vegetation, probing leaves and stems with its bill and picking prey from exposed surfaces. It may also seize small organisms from shallow water and muddy margins.
value.behavior: This jacana is usually active during daylight and is often seen walking deliberately across lily pads and other floating plants. It is territorial, especially during breeding, and may give sharp calls while displaying or chasing intruders. Females commonly defend territories that overlap the ranges of several males. When disturbed, the bird may fly low over the wetland and land among dense vegetation. Its long toes distribute its weight and help it avoid sinking through floating leaves.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be facing a rapid decline, although local numbers may vary with wetland conditions and habitat changes.
